questions.question: What is the main advantage of writing an addon with Node-API instead of raw V8 APIs?
options: It is ABI-stable, so a compiled addon keeps loading on later Node versions without recompiling
It lets addons run in the browser
It removes the need for a C compiler
It automatically runs all code on worker threads
questions.explanation: Node-API is an ABI-stable C interface; raw V8 or NAN addons must be rebuilt for every major Node version.

questions.question: A Node-API function takes 300 ms of CPU time and is called directly from JavaScript. What happens?
options: It runs on the libuv thread pool automatically
It blocks the event loop for 300 ms, because native code called from JavaScript runs on the main thread
Node kills the call after 100 ms
It runs in a separate process
questions.explanation: Native calls run on the main thread; long work should use napi_create_async_work so the execute step runs on the thread pool.

questions.question: Inside the execute callback of napi_create_async_work, what must you avoid?
options: Calling Node-API functions or touching JavaScript values
questions.explanation: execute runs on a thread-pool thread, where JavaScript values and Node-API calls are not allowed; copy inputs into C memory first and finish in the complete callback.

questions.question: Why might a team choose WebAssembly over a native addon?
options: Wasm calls have zero boundary cost, even for millions of tiny calls
Wasm can call any operating-system API directly
Wasm is always faster than native code
One .wasm file runs on every OS and CPU, and its sandbox means a bug cannot corrupt the Node process
questions.explanation: Wasm is portable and sandboxed to its own memory and imports; it does have a boundary cost, and native addons remain the most capable option.
